title: C++ Templates
relevance: Templates underpin the STL and are a central C++ interview topic: compile-time code generation, specialisation, headers, and constraints.

phases.goal: Establish that templates are compile-time blueprints that stamp out concrete typed code, not runtime constructs.

must_hit.point: A template is a stencil/blueprint for generating classes or functions; it is not runnable code on its own.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares it to a cookie cutter or stencil and says the template itself is not the executable function/class.

must_hit.point: On instantiation, the compiler substitutes template arguments into parameters and generates a separate ordinary concrete function or class per type set in the binary.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains that calling with int and double produces two completely separate stamped-out functions at compile time.

must_hit.point: C++ needs templates because of strict static typing; Python can duck-type a single runtime function for any object supporting the needed operators.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts Python runtime duck typing with C++ compile-time generation of distinct typed functions.

probes: What is a C++ template, and when does the compiler actually generate runnable code from it?
How does template instantiation differ from Python’s duck-typed generic functions?

hints.1: Think about whether the template itself runs, or something else does.
hints.2: Describe what the compiler does when it sees a call with specific argument types.
hints.3: A template is a compile-time stencil; each instantiation (e.g. int vs double) stamps out a separate concrete function in the binary.

phases.goal: Cover function/class templates, deduction, dependent typename, non-type/default parameters, specialisation, and variadic packs.

must_hit.point: In a template parameter list, typename and class mean the same thing; typename is the conventional preference for generic types.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says the two forms are entirely equivalent and notes typename is preferred in modern style while class appears in older code.

must_hit.point: The compiler usually deduces T from call arguments; conflicting deductions fail, and explicit arguments like add<double>(...) force the type and allow conversion.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives an example where mixed double/int deduction conflicts, then shows explicit <double> fixing it.

must_hit.point: Function templates may be overloaded with ordinary functions; a perfect-match ordinary function is preferred, and display<> forces the template.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks through display(42) hitting the ordinary int overload, display(3.14) instantiating the template, and display<>(42) forcing the template.

must_hit.point: typename is required when naming a nested type that depends on a template parameter (e.g. Container::const_iterator), to tell the compiler it is a type.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains dependent nested types need typename so they are not treated as static data members.

must_hit.point: Class-template members defined outside the class must repeat the template header and use the full scope name like Box<T>::.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows template <typename T> T Box<T>::getContent() const { ... }.

must_hit.point: Non-type template parameters can be compile-time constants (e.g. std::size_t N) used as fixed sizes; template parameters can also have defaults.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions FixedArray<T, N> with N as a compile-time size and Buffer with defaults equivalent to Buffer<int, 10> when written Buffer<>.

must_hit.point: Full specialisation uses empty template <> and a concrete type; partial specialisation keeps some parameters generic (e.g. T*) and is allowed only for class templates, not function templates.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts Printer<bool> full specialisation with PointerPrinter<T*> partial specialisation and states partial is class-only.

must_hit.point: Variadic templates (C++11) use parameter packs (...); historically unpacked via recursive peeling plus a base case, while C++17 fold expressions reduce a pack over a binary operator.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes printAll recursion with sizeof...(args) and sumAll using (... + args) as a fold.

probes: How does template argument deduction work, and how do you resolve a conflict?
When must you write typename before a nested name like Container::const_iterator?
What is the difference between full and partial specialisation, and which applies to function templates?

hints.1: Start with how the compiler picks T from the call site.
hints.2: Separate deduction/overloading, dependent-type typename, then specialisation and packs.
hints.3: Deduce T from args or use explicit <T>; prefer perfect-match non-templates; require typename for dependent nested types; full specialisation is template<> for one type, partial keeps some parameters and is class-only; packs unpack recursively or with C++17 folds.

phases.goal: Contrast specialisation styles, constraint mechanisms, and where template definitions must live.

must_hit.point: Full specialisation replaces the entire stencil for one concrete type; partial specialisation customises a pattern (e.g. all T*) while leaving other parameters open—and only for class templates.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares a complete Printer<bool> override with a PointerPrinter<T*> pattern and notes function templates use overloading instead of partial specialisation.

must_hit.point: SFINAE silently discards invalid substitutions instead of hard-erroring; C++20 Concepts give a direct, readable way to state the same kinds of constraints.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines Substitution Failure Is Not An Error and positions Concepts as the modern replacement for ad-hoc SFINAE constraints.

must_hit.point: Because of the separate-compilation model, template declarations and definitions must live together in headers; hiding the body in a .cpp prevents instantiation and causes linker failures.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says the compiler needs the full definition at the instantiation site, so .h/.hpp holds both declaration and definition.

probes: Why do template definitions belong in headers rather than .cpp files?
When would you use full specialisation versus partial specialisation?
How do Concepts relate to older SFINAE-based constraints?

hints.1: Ask what the compiler must see when it stamps out a type.
hints.2: Compare specialised overrides, pack/constraint styles, and the header vs translation-unit split.
hints.3: Full = one concrete type via template<>; partial = pattern like T*, class-only; SFINAE discards bad substitutions, Concepts declare constraints; definitions must be in headers or the linker misses symbols.

phases.goal: Apply templates to interview explanations: generation model, specialisation choice, and header placement.

must_hit.point: In interviews, state clearly that templates are compile-time code generators, not runtime polymorphism or duck typing.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Leads with “compile-time stencil / code generation” and rejects “runtime generic function” wording.

must_hit.point: Be ready to articulate full versus partial specialisation and why template definitions must be in headers, not separately compiled .cpp files.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives a crisp full-vs-partial contrast and ties header placement to instantiation and linker errors.

must_hit.point: Use ordinary overloads for perfect matches, specialisation when a type needs a different implementation, and Concepts (or historically SFINAE) when you need to constrain which types may instantiate.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps overload preference, Printer/bool-style specialisation, and Concepts/SFINAE to concrete design choices.

probes: Explain templates as if answering a C++ interview: what are they, how do specialisations differ, and why headers?
Given a type that needs different printing behaviour and a constrained generic algorithm, which tools would you reach for?

hints.1: Lead with compile-time generation, then specialisation and headers.
hints.2: Structure: what stamps out code → full vs partial → where definitions live → constraints.
hints.3: Templates generate typed code at compile time; full specialisation overrides one type, partial a pattern (classes only); put full definitions in headers; constrain with Concepts (or SFINAE).

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Full specialisation (template <> for a concrete type) replaces the whole implementation for that type; partial specialisation keeps some parameters generic (e.g. T*) and is only allowed on class templates—function templates use overloading instead.

tradeoffs.topic: Ordinary function overload vs function template
tradeoffs.strong_answer: If an ordinary non-template function is a perfect match, the compiler prefers it; otherwise it instantiates the template. Syntax like display<> forces the template path even when an ordinary overload exists.

tradeoffs.topic: Recursive pack expansion vs fold expressions
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Pre-C++17 style peels a parameter pack with a recursive template plus base case; C++17 fold expressions reduce the pack over a binary operator and remove that boilerplate.
SFINAE discards templates whose substitution yields invalid code, historically used to constrain instantiations; C++20 Concepts state those constraints directly in a readable language feature.

The compiler must see the full template definition at each instantiation site; putting only a declaration in a header and the body in a .cpp breaks separate compilation and leads to linker errors, so both live in .h/.hpp.

gotchas.trap: Placing template definitions in a .cpp while only declaring them in a header.
gotchas.correction: Keep declaration and definition together in a header so every instantiation site can stamp out concrete code; otherwise the linker cannot find the symbols.

gotchas.trap: Assuming the compiler fully type-checks template bodies before any instantiation.
gotchas.correction: Template code is not fully checked until it is actually instantiated.

gotchas.trap: Trying to partially specialise a function template.
gotchas.correction: Partial specialisation is only for class templates; function templates rely on overloading instead.

gotchas.trap: Writing Container::const_iterator inside a template without typename.
gotchas.correction: A nested name that depends on a template parameter needs typename so the compiler treats it as a type, not a static member.

gotchas.trap: Calling a single-parameter function template with arguments of conflicting deduced types.
gotchas.correction: Deduction must agree for T; use an explicit template argument (e.g. add<double>(...)) so conversions can reconcile the call.
